“Who is the traitor?”: Babu and Sifuna clash over who leads Linda Mwananchi
items.description: Edwin Sifuna and Babu Owino trade accusations over who broke the original Linda Mwananchi deal, as a leadership dispute deepens within the political movement.
content: The newspapers Friday, November 20, covered an array of topics, including the growing political feud between Linda Mwananchi leader and Nairobi senator Edwin Sifuna and The Mwananchi Party leader and Embakasi East Babu Owino.
PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

The newspaper reported on a public spat between Nairobi senator Edwin Sifuna and Embakasi East MP Babu Owino having escalated into a full-blown dispute over who betrayed whom within the Linda Mwananchi Movement, with both politicians offering conflicting accounts of what was originally agreed.

Sifuna broke his silence on Thursday during an interview on Radio Citizen's Jambo Kenya programme, responding directly to accusations Babu made on November 13, in which the MP claimed their initial understanding was that Sifuna would contest the presidency while Babu chaired the party.
Babu told listeners that the arrangement shifted later without his knowledge.

Sifuna denied that characterisation, telling the same programme that the founding agreement was simpler: each leader would leave their individual party and join a single platform that could advance their shared political goals.
After reviewing available parties, the group settled on The Equitable Party (TEP) , which was later renamed Linda Mwananchi Movement.
He named South Suba MP Caroli Omondi, former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza, and Mavoko MP Patrick Makau among those who abandoned their former parties to join the new vehicle.
Omondi had previously served under ODM, Makau under Kalonzo Musyoka's Wiper Patriotic Front, and Mwangaza under Umoja na Maendeleo Party.

Sifuna said the group convened to discuss the party's leadership structure and collectively chose him to lead as both party chair and presidential candidate, insisting the outcome was not self-imposed.
He challenged Babu's suggestion by questioning whether any political party in Kenya runs its presidential candidate separately from its party leadership.
Edwin Sifuna swears by the Bible as he addresses disagreement with Babu Owino, other leaders

Tensions between the two leaders first surfaced openly in September, when Babu announced he would scale back his attendance at Linda Mwananchi gatherings to focus on his gubernatorial bid for Nairobi County.
Babu has consistently downplayed suggestions of rivalry, arguing the two are chasing different offices, but the exchange of accusations points to a more fundamental breakdown in trust.

Political analysts have noted that if Sifuna consolidates opposition support for a presidential run, Nairobi's governorship could become a bargaining chip in broader coalition negotiations, which may complicate Babu's own ambitions.

The fallout within the movement extends beyond the two principals. Siaya governor James Orengo has since joined the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) after distancing himself from Sifuna's camp, following internal resistance to Sifuna's presidential aspirations. Saboti MP Caleb Amisi has also departed to establish his own outfit, the People's Renaissance Movement (PM).

The newspaper reported on the opposition leaders dramatically walking out of an election preparedness meeting convened by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), demanding sweeping reforms before the August 2027 general election.
Blow to Kalonzo as Sifuna welcomes leaders from Makueni, Machakos and Kitui: "Linda Ukambani"

The walkout, led by DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua , took place Thursday, November 11, after the opposition accused the IEBC of failing to consult stakeholders adequately on election preparations and of ignoring proposals to establish technical teams to examine electoral integrity concerns.

Former Chief Justice David Maraga, who accompanied the opposition delegation, said Kenyans deserve a clean and verifiable voters' register before the next election. The bloc called for an independent audit of the register to remove deceased persons, duplicate registrations, and ineligible voters.
On results transmission, the opposition proposed that each of the 290 constituencies, as well as the diaspora vote, should have its own dedicated server.
They further demanded that political parties, candidates, and media organisations be granted real-time visibility into results as they are relayed from polling stations.
The opposition also wants presidential results declared on the basis of figures announced at polling stations and constituencies, rather than being recalculated at a single national tallying centre.
Additional demands include strengthened electoral offence laws, with severe penalties for officials found to have altered results or interfered with election systems.
The bloc also called for full transparency in the procurement, testing, and auditing of electoral technology, as well as an open recruitment process for election officials.
ODM MP dismisses opinion poll placing Sifuna at par with Ruto ahead of 2027: “He is too small”
Ballot paper printing and custody were also flagged as areas requiring closer scrutiny.
Gachagua stated that the opposition could not continue participating in the meeting because the agenda did not address issues of public concern.
Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka said the delegation had attended in good faith but left unconvinced that the commission was prepared to operate independently and impartially.

IEBC chairperson Erastus Ethekon expressed regret over the opposition's decision to leave, maintaining that the commission had called the meeting specifically to brief stakeholders on its preparedness.
Ethekon disclosed that technology procurement, which was initiated in July, has been delayed by ongoing court proceedings.

The newspaper reported on the oncoming recruitment exercise for Police Constables scheduled for December 10 , running from 8 am to 5 pm at designated centres across all 47 counties in Kenya as announced by the National Police Service (NPS).
The advertisement signed by Inspector General Douglas Kanja Kirocho, sets out the eligibility criteria, application process, and warning against corrupt practices.
Caleb Amisi names politician Raila wanted as Nairobi senator in 2022: "Sifuna was not"

To qualify, candidates must be Kenyan citizens aged between 18 and 28 years, holding a valid National Identity Card and a minimum Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) grade of D+, with at least D+ in either English or Kiswahili.
Applicants must also be physically and medically fit, with no criminal record or pending criminal charges.

Height requirements set the minimum at 5 feet 8 inches for male candidates and 5 feet 3 inches for female candidates. Female applicants must not be pregnant at the time of recruitment or at any point during the entire training period.
The recruitment draws its legal authority from Articles 238, 239, 244 and 245 of the Constitution, alongside Articles 10, 27(8) and 232, as well as the National Police Service Act.

Prospective candidates are required to download the prescribed application form from the NPS websites, www.nationalpolice.go.ke, www.kenyapolice.go.ke, www.administrationpolice.go.ke, or www.dci.go.ke, or collect one from the nearest Huduma Centre.

Completed forms, together with originals and copies of academic certificates, a National Identity Card, and a birth certificate, must be presented at the designated recruitment centre on the day of recruitment.
All applicants must arrive at their respective centres by 8 am.
Edwin Sifuna’s close ally names 3 prominent people blocking registration of Linda Mwananchi Movement Party

The 423 recruitment centres are spread across sub-counties in all 47 counties, with venues ranging from stadiums and sports grounds to schools, police stations, and District County Commissioners' offices.
Examples include Kisauni Sub-County Police Headquarters in Mombasa and Moi Sports Centre Kasarani in Nairobi.

Candidates affiliated with the National Youth Service (NYS) are directed to report to NYS Headquarters in Ruaraka, which is listed as centre number 423. NYS candidates must additionally present a discharge certificate with a conduct rating of at least "GOOD."

The NPS stressed that the recruitment process is entirely free and open to all eligible candidates. Bribery, corruption, or the submission of false or misleading information to gain an advantage in the process constitutes a criminal offence.

Members of the public are encouraged to report any malpractice to the nearest police station or through the following channels: the toll-free number 0800 722 203, the emergency lines 996 and 911, or the hashtag #FichuaKwaDCI.
The NPS confirmed that all reports will be handled with strict confidentiality.

items.title: End of an era? Kenya’s 'established' politicians face relevance test before 2027
items.description: Younger politicians are increasingly positioning themselves as alternatives to established...
content: Siaya Governor James Orengo (left) and Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka.
For decades, Kenya’s political landscape has been dominated by familiar faces whose influence has survived successive administrations, shifting alliances, political betrayals and electoral defeats.

But as the country edges towards the August 2027 General Election, a generational question is increasingly confronting some of its most experienced political operators: are they approaching the end of their era, or can they reinvent themselves in a political order increasingly demanding new faces, fresh ideas and a different style of leadership?

From Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi and National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula to Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka, Cooperatives Cabinet Secretary Wycliffe Oparanya, People’s Liberation Party chief Martha Karua, ODM leader Dr Oburu Oginga and Governor James Orengo (Siaya) and Boni Khalwale (Kakamega), the established political class is facing a changing environment in which age, succession, political relevance and the growing assertiveness of younger voters, pundits say, are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

“The challenge is not necessarily that these leaders have run out of political capital. Many retain extensive networks, institutional experience, regional influence and the ability to negotiate their way into powerful political arrangements. Rather, the question is whether the political structures that sustained their influence for decades, and age, can withstand the growing appetite for generational change,” political analyst Geoffrey Mboya says.
Also Read: Ruto courts Gen Z, vows to hand over power to young leaders in 2032
Moses Wetang'ula (left) and Musalia Mudavadi.

That tension is already playing out in Western Kenya, where some of the region’s most seasoned political figures have rallied behind Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna’s presidential ambitions, effectively challenging the established political order represented by Mr Mudavadi and Mr Wetang’ula.

The endorsement by former Cabinet ministers Musikari Kombo, Fred Gumo, Noah Wekesa and Philip Masinde, alongside former MPs Joash Wamang’oli and Bifwoli Wakoli, illustrates an unusual political development: veterans who once shaped the region’s leadership choices are now advocating for a younger politician to take the baton.

Mr Mboya argues that the development is significant because these are not political newcomers seeking relevance through a youthful candidate, but are “men who served in successive governments, worked with influential political figures and participated in shaping the political direction of the country for decades.”
Their argument is that Western Kenya must begin preparing a new generation for national leadership rather than remain dependent on leaders whose political careers began in a different era.

Deputy Party Leader of Democracy for the Citizen’s Party Cleophas Malala recently caused a stir at Mr Sifuna’s rally in Western when he publicly urged Dr Khalwale to retire alongside his peers and let the young generation take the driver’s seat, drawing violent reaction from the Kakamega Senator.

The developments expose a changing political conversation in a region where leadership has traditionally revolved around established political personalities, negotiated alliances and the influence of community elders.

But the generational debate is not confined to Western Kenya alone. Across the country, younger politicians are increasingly positioning themselves as alternatives to established political figures, challenging their parties’ internal hierarchies and attempting to build independent political identities.
Kakamega Senator Boni Khalwale and DCP deputy leader Cleophas Malala during the burial of Gloria Sekeiyan Khalwale in Malinya, Ikolomani Constituency, Kakamega County, on August 21, 2026.
Also Read: Western old guards abandon Mudavadi, Wetang’ula for Sifuna

The pattern is also evident in the opposition, where the contest over who should carry the presidential ticket has exposed tensions between veteran politicians and a younger crop seeking to redefine the country's political leadership.
Mr Musyoka, 72, has intensified his national mobilisation as he positions himself for another opportunity to contest the presidency.

Having served as Vice-President under the late President Mwai Kibaki, Mr Musyoka remains one of the most experienced opposition figures, with a political career stretching back to his election to Parliament in 1985.

But his ambitions are unfolding against the backdrop of an opposition increasingly under pressure to accommodate younger politicians, some of whom argue that the country needs a departure from familiar presidential candidates.

The generational question has also complicated the political calculations of Ms Karua, who has remained an important figure in opposition politics, and Mr Orengo, whose political career stretches back to the struggle for multiparty democracy.
The age factor makes the debate even more consequential.
An examination of the publicly available birth records of some of these politicians shows that several will be approaching or have crossed their eighth decade by the time Kenyans vote in August 2032.

The figures do not determine their political capacity, advocate Chris Omore argues, “but they illustrate the narrowing window within which some could pursue another presidential or major elective ambition.”
The IEBC has scheduled the next General Election for August 10, 2027. If the five-year electoral cycle remains unchanged, the subsequent election will be held in August 2032.

The figures are particularly striking for Dr Oginga, who will be 83 during the 2027 election and 88 in 2032, while Mr Orengo will be 76 and 81 respectively. Mr Musyoka, meanwhile, will be 73 in 2027 and 78 five years later.
Mr Mudavadi and Mr Wetang’ula, who have traditionally been regarded as the senior political figures in Western Kenya, will be 66 and 70 respectively in 2027. By 2032, they will be 71 and 75.
“At 71, Mudavadi could still be able run around, but that will depend on how the youthful leaders conduct themselves post 2027 election,” Mr Omore says.

For the veteran politicians, the implications extend beyond the numerical question of age. The 2027 election could represent their last realistic opportunity to pursue certain political ambitions before the next electoral cycle presents a considerably different set of circumstances.
Also Read: Sifuna - How my life has changed after Raila

For those interested in the presidency, the calculations are particularly difficult. A politician who fails to secure a ticket in 2027 would have to consider whether to wait another five years, support a younger candidate or negotiate a political arrangement that allows him to retain influence without necessarily occupying the highest office.
Former Nairobi Governor Mike Sonko recently illustrated this dilemma when he challenged Mr Musyoka to reconsider his options should the opposition deny him its presidential ticket.
Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, accompanied by party officials, addresses the media in Nairobi on October 19, 2026.

“This is his last bullet and his last chance. If the Opposition does not give him the opportunity to be its presidential flagbearer, he should not gamble again. He would be better off becoming Ruto’s Deputy President or Prime Minister,” Mr Sonko said in an interview with NTV last week.

The debate has also acquired another dimension following President William Ruto's remarks that he intends to leave active politics alongside some opposition chiefs including Mr Musyoka and former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua in 2032.

Speaking during his Gusii region tour on November 10, Dr Ruto described the politicians as belonging to his generation and suggested that they should make way for younger leaders after the next electoral cycle.

Although the President's remarks were politically charged, they captured a question increasingly confronting the established political class: whether the next five years should be spent consolidating their remaining influence or preparing a transition to a younger generation.

Mr Musyoka has not indicated that he intends to abandon his presidential ambitions, while other veteran politicians are equally unlikely to surrender their political positions simply because younger leaders are emerging.
In fact, Mr Orengo has just unveiled his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), on whose ticket he plans to reorganise his political ambitions.

For Mr Mudavadi and Mr Wetang’ula, the dilemma is slightly different. Both remain influential figures within government, with institutional positions that give them access to the national political conversation.
Their challenge is how to maintain their influence in Western Kenya while younger leaders increasingly demand a greater role in determining the region's political direction.
Also Read: ‘You did not make me president,’ Ruto tells Gachagua as he questions DCP leader’s conduct

The endorsement of Mr Sifuna by former Cabinet ministers and MPs, analysts say, suggests that even some of the region's established political networks are beginning to accommodate a different leadership proposition.
Mr Mboya, however cautions against outright dismissal of the older leaders.

“The old guard retains extensive political experience, established connections, financial networks and relationships with political parties that younger aspirants may struggle to replicate. Their experience in coalition negotiations, presidential campaigns and government provides them with advantages that cannot simply be measured by age,” he says.
Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro and Embakasi East MP Babu Owino.

The politicians challenging this established order include Mr Sifuna, Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro, Embakasi East MP Babu Owino, Nyandarua Senator John Methu, Kirinyaga Woman Representative Njeri Maina, Nyali MP Mohammed Ali and DCP deputy party leader Cleophas Malala, Vihiga Senator Godfrey Osotsi, Saboti MP Caleb Amisi, the late Raila Odinga’s daughter Winnie, who has declared interest in the Nairobi gubernatorial seat, among others.

Their emergence reflects a political environment in which younger leaders are increasingly seeking to influence party decisions, challenge established hierarchies and build political movements outside traditional political structures.

Mr Sifuna, who will be 45 in 2027, has become a central figure in the emerging generational contest through his Linda Mwananchi movement, which has attracted support from younger voters and politicians dissatisfied with the broad-based government arrangement.

Mr Nyoro, who is 40, has established himself as a prominent voice on economic policy, while Mr Owino has built a considerable following through his combative political style and mobilisation of urban voters.
The changing demographics of the electorate could further complicate the position of veteran politicians.

According to the Centre for Multiparty Democracy's 2026 People Dialogue Festival outcome report, young people aged between 18 and 35 account for approximately 57 per cent of eligible voters. The report emphasised their growing importance in electoral participation and accountability.

“However, the figures should not be interpreted as a guarantee that young voters will automatically support younger candidates. Their political preferences are diverse, and issues such as unemployment, taxation, the cost of living, corruption and accountability may matter more than the age of those seeking office,’ advocate Omore warns.
Frankline Mukwanja, Executive Director of the Centre for Multiparty Democracy, argues that younger politicians who are progressive and issue-oriented have a promising political future.
He cautions, however, that they must demonstrate an ability to organise independently and mobilise supporters beyond the established political machinery.

items.title: Mbadi, Oduor face sentencing over Kenya debt secrecy
items.description: National Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi and Attorney General Dorcas Oduor were yesterday found guilty of contempt of court by the High Court after failing to comply with orders requiring the government to disclose Kenya's sovereign bond agreements and account for how the borrowed funds were spent, with both officials now facing personal sentencing on 27 November 2026.
content: High Court finds Treasury CS and Attorney General in contempt for defying orders to disclose sovereign bond agreements and spending.

National Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi and Attorney General Dorcas Oduor were yesterday found guilty of contempt of court by the High Court after failing to comply with orders requiring the government to disclose Kenya’s sovereign bond agreements and account for how the borrowed funds were spent, with both officials now facing personal sentencing on 27 November 2026.

High Court Judge Patricia Nyaunndi delivered the ruling following a contempt application by the Kenya Human Rights Commission and activist Wanjiru Gikonyo, National Coordinator of the Institute for Social Accountability — the same petitioners who first took the government to court in April 2022 demanding transparency over Kenya’s mounting public debt. The ruling is as significant for what it says about the state of Kenya’s institutions as it is about the specific officials named: two of the country’s most senior law officers have been found to have defied a binding court order, and they will now answer for it personally.

The legal origins of Thursday’s ruling stretch back over four years. In early 2022, the Kenya Human Rights Commission and Gikonyo formally requested records of all sovereign bonds floated by the Kenyan state over the preceding nine years, anchoring their demand in Article 201 of the Constitution, which mandates openness and accountability in all matters of public finance. When the National Treasury ignored the request, the petitioners moved to the High Court. In December 2024, Justice Lawrence Mugambi ruled in their favour, declaring the government’s secrecy unconstitutional and giving the state 45 days to produce two categories of information: all sovereign bond agreements and contracts entered into by the Republic of Kenya, and a full breakdown of how the proceeds from those bonds were spent.

Nearly two years later, neither set of disclosures had been made. Justice Nyaunndi’s contempt ruling is the direct consequence of that silence. The court has ordered both Mbadi and Oduor to appear in person before the High Court at noon on 27 November for sentencing — a requirement that underscores the personal nature of the accountability the bench is now imposing. In a further measure of the court’s displeasure, it ruled that the costs of the contempt application will be borne by the two officials in their personal capacities, not by the taxpayer. The state will not be permitted to absorb the financial consequences of its own defiance.

The significance of that last point should not be understated. Ordering public officials to pay legal costs personally rather than through government funds is a deliberate and pointed signal from the judiciary — a statement that contempt of court is not an institutional inconvenience to be managed through public resources but a personal breach of legal obligation with personal consequences. For a government that has repeatedly tested the boundaries of judicial authority, the November 27 sentencing will be an important moment of institutional reckoning.

Kenya’s public debt has been one of the most contested political and economic issues of the past decade. The country’s total debt stock has grown substantially across successive administrations, financed in part through a series of sovereign bond issuances that have attracted scrutiny from civil society, economists and opposition politicians alike. Questions about how the proceeds of those bonds were deployed — which projects received funding, which contracts were awarded, on what terms and to whom — have remained largely unanswered in the public domain. The court orders at the centre of Thursday’s contempt ruling were specifically designed to force those answers into the open. That they were not complied with for nearly two years speaks to the depth of the government’s reluctance to subject its borrowing record to public scrutiny.

For the Kenya Human Rights Commission and Gikonyo, Thursday’s ruling represents a significant, if incomplete, vindication. The judiciary has confirmed that the government’s continued secrecy is not merely a matter of administrative delay but a wilful defiance of constitutional and court-mandated obligations. “The Constitution is clear,” Gikonyo has previously stated in relation to the case. “Openness and accountability in public finance are not aspirational — they are mandatory.” The contempt finding gives that position the full force of judicial authority.

What happens on 27 November will determine the next chapter of this confrontation. The sentencing options available to Justice Nyaunndi range from fines to, in principle, committal — though the latter would represent an extraordinary escalation in the relationship between the judiciary and the executive. More likely is a structured order requiring compliance within a fixed and final deadline, backed by the credible threat of further and more severe consequences for continued defiance.

For ordinary Kenyans, whose taxes service a debt whose full terms they have never been permitted to see, the case is not abstract. It concerns the basic right to know how public money has been borrowed, on what conditions and to what ends. The High Court has now said, twice and unambiguously, that the government must answer those questions. Whether it finally does so will be the measure of whether Kenya’s constitutional architecture means what it says.

items.description: Saudi Arabia maintains its Kenya visa ban despite no new Ebola cases, while the UAE reopens to Ugandans after 21 days, leaving Kenyan workers still stranded.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

Saudi Arabia is holding firm on its travel and visa suspension against Kenya even as the United Arab Emirates has begun reopening its doors to travellers from Uganda , exposing a sharp divide in how Gulf nations are responding to the Ebola outbreak that swept through East Africa.

The Saudi restrictions, which took effect on October 30, 2026, bar Saudi nationals from travelling to Kenya and block entry to anyone who has been in Kenya or any other Ebola-affected country within the 21 days before arriving in the kingdom.
US issues travel warning against top destination for thousands of Kenyan workers in Gulf
The measures apply regardless of whether a traveller transits through a third country.

Saudi authorities tied the restrictions to their own national health assessments, triggered after Kenya confirmed an imported Ebola case on October 6, 2026, involving a traveller who had entered from the Democratic Republic of the Congo via Uganda.

Kenya's last confirmed case was recorded on October 19, and the final patient was discharged on November 11, 2026. A 42-day countdown to an official Ebola-free declaration began on November 12 and is due to conclude on December 23, 2026, if no new cases arise.
Kenya's Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale has described the Saudi measures as "excessive" and "not backed by the current epidemiological situation".
The Foreign Ministry has characterised them as a "blanket, punitive measure" unsupported by evidence. Diplomatic talks with Riyadh are ongoing, but no shift in Saudi policy has been announced.

The UAE had imposed a comparable suspension in June 2026 covering Uganda, the DRC and South Sudan. On November 11, 2026, its National Emergency, Crisis and Disasters Management Authority, acting in coordination with health and identity authorities, lifted the restriction for Uganda alone .
UAE lifts visa ban on East African country, imposes strict 21-day entry condition
Ugandan nationals can now apply for UAE visas and gain entry provided at least 21 days have passed since leaving Uganda.
Students, embassy staff and diplomatic passport holders are exempt from the waiting period, while restrictions on the DRC and South Sudan remain active.
Uganda's Foreign Affairs Minister, Ambassador Adonia Ayebare, publicly thanked the UAE government for reconsidering the restrictions.
The continued Saudi ban carries real consequences.
More than 300 Kenyans who travelled to Saudi Arabia in search of work were turned back at entry points in early November.

The kingdom has long been a major destination for Kenyan domestic workers, healthcare professionals, drivers and construction labourers, and remittances from Saudi Arabia were already under strain in 2026.
The situation differs markedly with the UAE, which has not imposed a blanket ban on Kenyan nationals.
The Emirates recently extended its visa-on-arrival programme to include eligible Kenyans, keeping that corridor open.
Kenya's diplomatic path forward rests significantly on the countdown to the December 23 Ebola-free declaration, which would give Nairobi a firmer basis to press Riyadh for a formal review.
Saudi Arabia has not signalled, however, that a Kenyan declaration would automatically result in the lifting of its restrictions.

The Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) unveiled a reverse invoicing arrangement under which factories and other agricultural produce buyers can generate electronic tax invoices on behalf of small-scale farmers, removing the need for individual farmers to operate their own invoicing systems.
KRA Commissioner for Micro and Small Taxpayers George Obell announced the arrangement at the KRA Citizen Assembly, a taxpayer town hall held at Murang'a University on Tuesday, November 17, 2026.

Obell said the arrangement addresses a persistent challenge in agricultural supply chains where large processors deal with numerous smallholder suppliers who may lack the equipment, internet connectivity, or technical know-how to issue eTIMS invoices independently.

Under the arrangement, an approved buyer such as a dairy processor documents the transaction directly within eTIMS, capturing details including the quantity of produce received and the agreed price.

A dairy factory buying milk from smallholder farmers, for instance, can generate an invoice reflecting each delivery without requiring each farmer to maintain a separate invoicing system.
This benefits buyers as well, since the generated invoices serve as valid documentation to support expense claims when filing tax returns.
Before any buyer can use the system, KRA requires them to complete a Know Your Customer process and obtain explicit approval from the authority.
Farmers must give informed consent before invoices can be raised in their name, and they receive notifications by SMS or email each time a transaction is recorded.

Farmers can also independently monitor and validate invoices through their eTIMS dashboard.
Buyers are required to capture the farmer's KRA PIN, the quantity supplied, and the transaction price, and must maintain a full audit trail of all records.
KRA also stipulates that buyers must absorb the operational costs of the reverse invoicing functionality rather than passing them on to farmers.
The arrangement is not entirely new. KRA introduced reverse invoicing on December 27, 2024, initially capturing transactions worth KSh 800 million.
At that point, approximately 800 buyers had used the system to generate around 4,500 invoices for small suppliers.

The renewed push comes after KRA issued a public notice on November 10, 2025, confirming that from January 1, 2026, declared income and expenses in tax returns would be validated against eTIMS records.
That requirement exposed a documentation gap for businesses buying produce from farmers unable to issue compliant electronic invoices.

Reverse invoicing is positioned as one of several solutions, alongside eTIMS Lite services accessible through eCitizen and USSD, designed to draw informal and small-scale suppliers into the electronic tax framework.
Obell encouraged farmers encountering difficulties with the process to contact KRA offices or reach out through the authority's official communication channels for assistance.

items.title: Nairobi, Kisumu, Homa Bay, and Migori Top List of Counties With Highest New HIV Infections
items.description: Nairobi, Kisumu, Homa Bay, and Migori counties recorded the highest numbers of new HIV infections in Kenya, accounting for nearly a third of all new cases…
content: Nairobi, Kisumu, Homa Bay, and Migori counties recorded the highest numbers of new HIV infections in Kenya, accounting for nearly a third of all new cases reported nationwide, according to the latest National Syndemic Diseases Control Council report.
Data from the 2026 Kenya HIV Estimates reveals that out of the 13,936 new HIV infections recorded across the country over the past year, Nairobi County topped the chart with 1,516 new cases.
Kisumu County ranked second with 1,057 new infections, followed closely by Homa Bay County with 985 cases and Migori County with 970 cases.

Together, the top four counties recorded 4,528 new infections, underscoring persistent regional concentration of fresh transmission in the capital city and the Lake Victoria basin despite an overall 30 per cent decline in annual infections nationwide.

A demographic breakdown of the new infections shows that adult women bore a disproportionate share of fresh cases, with 7,363 new infections recorded among women aged 15 years and above compared to 3,177 among men.

Young people aged between 15 and 24 years accounted for 4,322 new infections, while adolescents aged between 10 and 19 years recorded 2,077 new cases and children aged 14 years and below accounted for 3,396 new infections.

In terms of cumulative population living with HIV across all 47 counties, 10 high burden counties account for nearly 60 per cent of the estimated 1,481,853 Kenyans living with the virus, led by Nairobi at 189,640, Homa Bay at 128,906, Kisumu at 114,986, Siaya at 96,304, and Migori at 80,105.

Busia, Kakamega, Mombasa, Kiambu, and Nakuru complete the top 10 counties with the highest cumulative HIV populations, while arid and northern counties including Lamu, Wajir, and Mandera recorded the lowest infection numbers nationwide.

The National Syndemic Diseases Control Council urged county governments to intensify targeted community testing, treatment retention, and youth prevention campaigns to curb new infections ahead of the 2030 elimination target.

items.title: Kenya Construction Regulator Flags Inspection Gaps After 72 Collapses
items.description: Kenya's National Construction Authority covers only 27 counties with five Nairobi inspectors after 72 building collapses in three years, amid heavy rains.
content: Kenya's National Construction Authority covers only 27 counties with five Nairobi inspectors after 72 building collapses in three years, amid heavy rains.

Kenya's National Construction Authority has warned that severe underfunding leaves it operating in only 27 of the country's 47 counties, even after 72 buildings collapsed nationwide over the past three years.

According to a November 19, 2026 Citizen TV report and a November 20 Kenyans.co.ke update, the regulator faces acute staffing constraints as seasonal heavy rainfall heightens structural risks across active construction zones. In Nairobi, the epicentre of Kenya's high-rise development boom, only five NCA inspection officers are tasked with overseeing thousands of ongoing projects.

The disclosure exposes a central contradiction in Kenya's built environment: while the state replaced a 56-year-old colonial building order in February 2025 with the National Building Code, 2024, front-line capacity to verify whether developers follow those rules has fallen far behind the pace of urban construction.

Leaving 20 Kenyan counties without an NCA operational footprint forces regulators to stretch sparse teams across wide regions or rely on reactive checks after failures occur. With only five inspectors assigned to Nairobi's entire construction pipeline, routine site verification across excavation, foundation curing, concrete mixing, and multi-storey framing becomes physically impossible at scale.

The human stakes of inspection gaps were underscored in Eastleigh, Nairobi, where an 18-storey building collapsed in October 2026. On November 5, the fourteenth day of search and rescue operations, Citizen TV reported that teams recovered six additional bodies, bringing the confirmed death toll to eight while five people remained unaccounted for and families waited for answers.

Increased rainfall across Kenya adds immediate physical stress to compromised structures. Waterlogged soils reduce bearing capacity under shallow or poorly engineered foundations, while unsealed concrete slabs and inadequate drainage accelerate structural degradation on stalled or hurried sites.

Preventing structural failures requires coordination across multiple laws and institutions rather than a single agency acting alone. Under Kenya's statutory framework, responsibility is divided between county governments and national regulators at distinct stages of a project's life cycle.

In practice, that split creates dangerous seams. County governments issue initial development permissions and approve architectural and structural plans under the Physical and Land Use Planning Act. The NCA, established under Act No. 41 of 2011, registers contractors, accredits site supervisors and skilled workers, registers projects, and monitors compliance on active sites.

When county plan-vetting, NCA site registration, and physical inspections fail to align, unauthorised floors, unverified design changes, or unapproved occupancy can persist undetected until a structure fails. Published in Kenya Gazette No. 28 on March 1, 2024 and commenced on February 20, 2025, the National Building Code, 2024 replaced the 1968 Local Government Building Order with updated rules on structural design, fire protection, electrical installations, occupancy certification, and enforcement. Yet updated legal standards cannot inspect concrete pours on their own.

Even when inspectors flag violations, the gap between legal authority and sustained enforcement remains wide across fast-growing neighbourhoods. Developers face intense commercial pressure to finish multi-storey residential blocks quickly and occupy ground floors before upper levels or certification procedures are complete.

Public records reviewed from the November 19 and November 20 briefings do not disclose the exact size of the NCA's current funding shortfall in shillings, nor has the regulator published a county-by-county breakdown identifying where the 72 collapses occurred or how many resulted in criminal convictions.

Under the National Construction Authority Act, contractors, site supervisors, and skilled construction workers must hold accreditation, and ongoing projects must be registered before works proceed. However, without enough county offices or inspectors to verify compliance on the ground, registration risks remaining a paper formality rather than an active safety filter.

For prospective tenants, buyers, and lenders, the practical baseline is clear: verifying both county development approvals and NCA project registration before committing money remains essential, yet self-checks cannot substitute for state inspections. Until Kenya matches its 2024 Building Code with funded inspectors across all 47 counties, heavy rains and rapid high-rise construction will continue to test weak links in the regulatory chain.

items.title: “We’ve Been Fooled”: Olympian Questions Kenya’s Marathon Dominance After Another Doping Scandal
items.description: Jimmy Gressier questions Kenya’s marathon dominance after Peres Jepchirchir’s suspension sparks fresh doping concerns.
content: When Veronica Loleo and Ronald Korir received doping bans, it was a big blow to Kenya’s distance running. But the situation became even more concerning when one of the country’s biggest stars, Olympic champion Peres Jepchirchir, was also handed a three-year suspension after testing positive for EPO. With the number of Kenyan athletes facing doping sanctions continuing to grow, questions are now being raised about the country’s long-standing dominance in distance running. And French Olympic runner Jimmy Gressier is among those who are no longer staying silent.

Gressier, who became the 10,000m world champion in 2025, reacted on November 19, the same day Jepchirchir’s three-year ban was officially announced. Although the Kenyan had initially denied the doping allegations, she later admitted to the violations and accepted the suspension. Gressier shared his reaction through a series of Instagram stories and videos, first posting the news with a sarcastic remark: “Waaah, waaah, the Kenyans are the best in the world. Luckily there are still clean athletes to save the day.” But that was only the beginning of his criticism.

In a message addressed to the media, Gressier spoke about the financial struggles faced by many Kenyan athletes. While he said he could understand the difficult circumstances they live in, he made it clear that this could never excuse doping. “Even if I understand that these Kenyan athletes live in poverty, that doesn’t excuse cheating. These are moments of life that are stolen by cheaters,” he wrote.

He went on to explain why he believed financial pressure could play a part in some athletes’ decisions. “Kenyan or African athlete living in poverty might dope than a European athlete who has other alternatives to succeed in life than cheating in sport,” Gressier said. However, his criticism went beyond the circumstances that might lead someone to cheat.

In a series of videos, he openly questioned Kenya’s reputation as a country that consistently produces the world’s best distance runners. “We’ve been told for a long time that Kenyan athletes are the best in the world, blah blah blah… What I think is that’s false. I think that for quite a few years, we’ve been fooled by the cheating of these athletes,” he said.

Gressier did acknowledge that Kenya has plenty of genuinely talented runners who are passionate about the sport. “There are very talented, very strong Kenyan athletes, very willing to run because it’s the number one sport there. There’s no problem with that,” he said. But he also claimed that some agents were taking advantage of athletes’ financial struggles to make money from doping. “For these athletes, this represents considerable income compared to what they could earn working in Kenya, because the poverty level is truly extreme compared to what we experience in Europe,” he said.

Gressier also pointed out that European athletes often have access to free education and other career opportunities, making him less understanding of those who choose to dope. He was careful to explain that he was not dismissing the talent of Kenyan runners, but he wanted the sport to be fair to everyone who competes cleanly. He ended with a message about the values he believes athletics should protect: “Sport is above all the essence of hard work and meritocracy; it’s extremely important to preserve that.”

What makes the situation even more troubling is the scale of the problem. According to The Guardian, more than 320 Kenyan athletes faced sanctions since the Athletics Integrity Unit was established in 2017. With new cases continuing to emerge and several high-profile marathon runners among those punished, concerns are growing that Kenya could once again face the threat of wider international sanctions. And this would not be the first time the country has come close to such a situation.

Kenya faced the threat of an international athletics ban before in 2022. At the time, 55 Kenyan athletes were serving doping suspensions, while another eight were provisionally suspended. The growing number of cases raised concerns within World Athletics, and Kenya was at risk of being barred from international competitions. However, the country managed to avoid that punishment after its government promised to invest $25 million over five years to strengthen its anti-doping programme.

The funding was intended to support more testing, investigations, additional staff and anti-doping education. But the problem has continued despite those efforts. According to The Irish Times , 148 Kenyan athletes were serving active doping bans in athletics as of late October 2026. The report also revealed that Peres Jepchirchir became the ninth Kenyan among 10 World Marathon Major winners to receive a doping suspension since 2017.

With more athletes facing punishment, Kenya’s reputation is once again under pressure. The timing is particularly concerning because the country is preparing to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships in Nairobi, marking the first time the competition will be held in Africa. The growing doping controversy has also brought greater attention to whether Kenya can provide a clean sporting environment for the event.

Despite these concerns, Kenya’s success in athletics has not disappeared. At the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, the country finished second in the overall medal standings, winning seven gold medals, two silver medals and two bronze medals. Its athletes continue to achieve major victories on the international stage, but repeated doping cases are making it harder to separate those achievements from the questions surrounding the country’s anti-doping record.

Kenya did manage to avoid another set of proposed sanctions from the World Anti-Doping Agency in 2025 after agreeing to corrective measures. Its national anti-doping agency was eventually removed from WADA’s compliance watchlist in February 2026. However, with fresh cases involving high-profile runners such as Jepchirchir, concerns have returned. If the country fails to address the growing doping problem and meet international anti-doping requirements, it could once again face the threat of sanctions, including restrictions that could affect its participation in international athletics competitions.

CAF Unveils Shield-Inspired PAMOJA 2027 Logo as Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda Prepare to Host Africa Cup of Nations
items.description: The Confederation of African Football (CAF), together with hosts Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, has launched the official logo of the TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations 2027, unveiling a shield-inspired emblem that…
content: The Confederation of African Football (CAF), together with hosts Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, has launched the official logo of the TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations 2027, unveiling a shield-inspired emblem that will carry the branding PAMOJA 2027 for the first finals of the continent's flagship football tournament to be staged across three nations.

CAF said the design is inspired by the shield, which the continental football body described as "a timeless symbol deeply rooted in African heritage, identity and strength". The emblem becomes the public face of a tournament that will be shared by the three East African neighbours under the PAMOJA name, the Swahili word for together, and it was presented jointly by CAF and the three host nations at the launch.

Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda secured the 2027 hosting rights through a joint bid approved by the CAF Executive Committee in 2023, the same decision-making process that awarded the 2025 finals to Morocco. The award returned the Africa Cup of Nations to East Africa for the first time since Ethiopia staged the 1976 edition, and the bid was built around matches being played across all three countries under a single shared tournament identity.

While the competition has previously been co-hosted, with Ghana and Nigeria sharing the 2000 finals and Gabon and Equatorial Guinea staging the 2012 edition together, the 2027 tournament is the first Africa Cup of Nations to be shared by three countries. The arrangement follows football's broader shift toward joint hosting, after the 2026 FIFA World Cup was staged across the United States, Mexico and Canada.

The launch confirms the full official title of the event as the TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations PAMOJA 2027, with French energy group TotalEnergies continuing in its long-running role as the tournament's title sponsor. First contested in 1957, the Africa Cup of Nations is held every two years and brings together 24 national teams to decide the continental champion, with the most recent edition hosted by Morocco.

The shield was chosen for its resonance far beyond the pitch. Shields feature on the national coats of arms of Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, and the symbol recurs across African traditions of ceremony, identity and defence, aligning with the qualities of heritage and strength that CAF attached to the new design.

The unveiling opens the public-facing countdown to the finals, with the new identity set to anchor the tournament's marketing, broadcast presentation and merchandise in the build-up to 2027. Attention now turns to operational preparations across the three host countries, with organisers due to release details on venues, match schedules and ticketing arrangements in the coming months.

National teams across the continent are engaged in the qualification campaign for the 24-team finals, while Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda prepare to stage the competition as hosts. CAF is expected to announce further tournament details, including the match schedule and the draw for the finals, as the countdown to the PAMOJA 2027 edition continues.

items.title: Kenya flags off 8 students for Huawei’s Global ICT Programme
items.description: Kenya has officially flagged off eight competitively selected Kenyan university students participating in the 2026 edition of Huawei’s flagship global Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiative, Seeds for the Future. The eight Kenyan delegates will travel to Dongguan and Shenzhen, China, for an intensive, fully funded technical immersion.- Advertisement - During their stay, the students will […]
content: Kenya has officially flagged off eight competitively selected Kenyan university students participating in the 2026 edition of Huawei’s flagship global Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiative, Seeds for the Future.
The eight Kenyan delegates will travel to Dongguan and Shenzhen, China, for an intensive, fully funded technical immersion.

During their stay, the students will gain hands-on training at Huawei’s state-of-the-art research and development facilities, mastering emerging technologies including Artificial Intelligence (AI), 5G and 6G networks, cloud computing, and digital power systems, while engaging in knowledge exchange with international peers.

Presiding over the ceremonial handover of the Kenya National Flag to the student delegation on Thursday, Principal Secretary, State Department for Foreign Affairs Dr. Korir Sing’Oei, representing the Prime Cabinet Secretary and Cabinet Secretary for Foreign and Diaspora Affairs, Musalia Mudavadi underscored the critical role of human capital development in national growth and global competitiveness.

“Education is the pathway for transformation, but only to the extent that we link education to markets, skills, and job creation. By enabling students of technology and leadership in Kenya to travel to Shenzhen and interact directly with a global technology powerhouse like Huawei, we are providing a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Huawei’s investment directly strengthens Nairobi’s position as a digital leader on the African continent,” he said.

The PS further noted that this initiative translates key commitments made during his official delegation visit to Huawei Headquarters in Shenzhen in August 2026 into tangible outcomes for Kenyan youth.

He highlighted that the initiative aligns with the Government’s Digital Superhighway agenda under the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) and reinforces the strategic bilateral friendship between the Republic of Kenya and the People’s Republic of China.
Speaking on behalf of Huawei Technologies Kenya, Sun Quan (James), Deputy Chief Executive Officer, reaffirmed Huawei’s commitment to nurturing local ICT talent.

“This program is named ‘Seeds for the Future.’ As these eight talented students visit Shenzhen to exchange ideas with global technical experts, our hope is that when they return, they will turn into ‘Big Trees’ that contribute significantly to Kenya’s digital economy and national development.”

Launched globally in 2008, Huawei’s Seeds for the Future program has cultivated tech talent across the globe, engaging nearly 19,800 students from 143 countries and building partnerships with over 500 universities worldwide.

The 2026 edition reinforces Huawei’s ongoing support for Kenya’s digital ecosystem, extending across private sector infrastructure, public sector capacity building, and advanced technical skills transfer.

The ceremony was attended by key government and industry leaders, including Amb. Jane B. Makori, Deputy Director General for Asia Affairs; Dr. Wahome Rureri, Deputy Director for Higher Education at the State Department for Higher Education; Khadija Mohamed Ahmed of Huawei Technologies; and student representative Ahmed Rashid from the University of Nairobi Faculty of Law, who delivered remarks on behalf of the selected cohort.

Glovo expands investment in Kenya with two new facilities, targets 1,000 additional riders by year-end
items.description: Glovo, a leading technology platform operating across Europe, Central Asia and Africa, has opened two new facilities in Nairobi as part of its KSh10 billion investment commitment in Kenya, reinforcing its focus on creating meaningful employment and income-generating opportunities for young Kenyans.
content: Glovo, a leading technology platform operating across Europe, Central Asia and Africa, has opened two new facilities in Nairobi as part of its KSh10 billion investment commitment in Kenya, reinforcing its focus on creating meaningful employment and income-generating opportunities for young Kenyans.

The new Real Time Operations (RTO) office and Glovo Centre mark another step in the company’s expansion in Kenya, following the opening of its regional office in Nairobi in May 2026, where Glovo announced plans to invest an additional KSh 10 billion in the country by 2030. The facilities are designed to strengthen Glovo’s operations while providing young people with opportunities to build careers, develop practical skills and improve their financial wellbeing.

The facilities were officially launched during a visit to Kenya by Glovo Co-founder, Sacha Michaud, who engaged with employees, riders and other stakeholders on the company’s growth plans and continued investment in the market.

Speaking during the launch, Michaud said, “When we announced our investment commitment earlier this year, our ambition was not simply to grow Glovo’s presence in Kenya, but to create more opportunities for people to earn, learn and build their futures. These new facilities are part of making that commitment a reality. We want young Kenyans working within our operations to have opportunities to develop their skills and grow their careers, while ensuring riders have access to the training and financial knowledge that can help them make the most of their earnings and pursue their own ambitions.”

The new Real Time Operations office reflects Kenya’s growing role as a hub for Glovo’s operations. Initially established to support six markets, the Nairobi-based department has significantly expanded its mandate and now provides round-the-clock operational support across 21 markets.

The expansion has also increased the office’s capacity from an initial 100 workstations to accommodate 220 staff members, with plans to significantly increase capacity further as operations grow. This investment is expected to create additional employment opportunities for young Kenyans, particularly those looking to build careers in technology-enabled operations and customer support.

Beyond employment, the RTO office provides an environment where young professionals can gain practical experience, develop operational and problem-solving skills, and build careers within Glovo’s wider business.
Alongside the RTO office, Glovo officially opened its first Glovo Centre in Kenya, a dedicated facility designed to bring rider onboarding, training, development and support services under one roof.

The Centre will provide riders with access to practical training and skills development opportunities, supporting them in managing their work on the platform while equipping them with knowledge that can be useful beyond deliveries, including in pursuing entrepreneurship and other income-generating opportunities.

To mark the opening, Glovo partnered with Centonomy to deliver a financial literacy training session for 50 riders, equipping them with practical financial management skills to help them better manage their earnings, develop a savings culture and plan for their financial futures.

The occasion also marked the launch of a rider-led Savings and Credit Cooperative Society (SACCO), established by Glovo riders themselves to encourage saving, improve access to credit and strengthen their financial wellbeing. Supported by Glovo, the initiative provides riders with an opportunity to collectively build financial security and access resources that can support their personal and entrepreneurial ambitions.

Through the new Glovo Centre, the company is targeting the onboarding of an additional 1,000 riders by the end of 2026, building on the 2,765 riders already onboarded in the first ten months of the year. The figure represents Glovo’s highest annual rider onboarding since entering the Kenyan market in 2019, reflecting its continued efforts to expand income-generating opportunities through the platform.

Since launching in Kenya in 2019, Glovo has grown to connect more than 6,000 businesses with customers through its platform, while over 12,400 riders have had the opportunity to earn income through deliveries.

The opening of the two facilities builds on Glovo’s long-term investment plans for Kenya, with a focus on expanding opportunities for young men and women to participate in the digital economy. Through employment, skills development, financial literacy and rider support initiatives, the company aims to ensure that its continued growth creates opportunities for people to build sustainable livelihoods and pursue their longer-term career and business ambitions.

items.title: Medical professionals sound alarm over antibiotic misuse, warn of rising drug resistance
items.description: Medical, dental and pharmaceutical associations are urging the government to tighten controls on antibiotic sales and prescriptions, warning that rising antimicrobial resistance could threaten Kenya's healthcare gains.
content: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Medical and pharmaceutical professionals have raised concern over the growing misuse of antibiotics in Kenya, warning that failure to regulate the use of antimicrobial medicines could undermine treatment of common infections and expose the country to a major public health crisis.

The Kenya Medical Association (KMA), Kenya Dental Association (KDA) and Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya (PSK) are calling for stricter controls on the sale and prescription of antibiotics, alongside expanded surveillance and public education to contain antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

In a joint statement marking World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week, observed from November 18 to 24, the three organisations warned that drug-resistant infections are increasingly threatening the effectiveness of medicines that have long been relied upon to save lives.

They said Kenya risked losing critical gains in healthcare if urgent measures were not taken to address the inappropriate use of antibiotics in hospitals, pharmacies, communities and the agricultural sector.

The professionals cited global estimates linking bacterial antimicrobial resistance to approximately 4.7 million deaths in 2021, with projections indicating that resistance could directly cause 39 million deaths worldwide between 2025 and 2050.

items.title: How to register for SHA in Kenya and access health services (a step-by-step guide)
items.description: Learn how to register for SHA in Kenya online, via *147# or at a Huduma Centre, what documents you need, how contributions work and how to access healthcare.
content: The Social Health Authority ( SHA ) replaced the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) and began operations on 1 October 2024. Missing out on SHA registration means you risk losing access to public healthcare at thousands of facilities across Kenya. This guide covers everything you need to register for SHA in Kenya — online, on your phone, or at a Huduma Centre — and start accessing health services.
How to apply for a HELB loan as a first-time applicant: Complete guide

SHA offers four registration methods: USSD via *147#, the online SHA portal, the official SHA mobile app, and in-person registration at Huduma Centres, SHA offices, or through Community Health Promoters.
The fastest route for most people is *147# — no smartphone, no portal queue. Follow these steps:
How to check the SHA payment status: 3 easy ways to confirm your health cover
SHA online registration in Kenya is done through the Afya Yangu portal — or via *147# on your phone. Here is how to register online:
Different ways to check motor insurance validity in Kenya
If you encounter difficulties during registration, you can seek help from a Community Health Promoter (CHP), visit a SHA branch, or visit a Huduma Centre near you.
There is no SHA registration fee charged by the government. However, monthly contributions are required to activate and maintain your cover.
Salaried employees: your employer deducts 2.75% of your gross pay (a minimum of KES 300) and remits it to SHA by the 9th of the following month.
Self-employed workers: complete the means test via 147# or Afya Yangu to set your household's monthly contribution — from a minimum of KES 300 * — then pay to activate your cover.
How to register a company in Kenya on the eCitizen portal
Self-employed and informal workers pay via M-Pesa Paybill 200222 , using your National ID number as the account number.

Level 1–3 facilities (dispensaries and health centres) offer free outpatient services through the Primary Healthcare Fund, while Level 4–6 hospitals provide access to specialised care, surgeries, and inpatient services.

When visiting a hospital, confirm the facility is empanelled with SHA for the service you need, present your ID for membership verification, and ask staff to confirm what is covered and whether any co-payment applies.

Register before you need treatment, not at the hospital. Use *147#, the portal, or the app to add a newborn, a new spouse, or remove a dependant — a dependant not registered may be turned away from covered services.
OTP not received or portal timed out: If your registration fails or hangs at the OTP stage, wait a few minutes and retry on *147#, since the portal can time out under heavy load.
How to apply for affordable housing in Kenya: A step-by-step guide
ID not found: Ensure you are entering your National ID number exactly as it appears on the card — no spaces or leading zeros omitted.
Former NHIF member: NHIF registration does not carry over to SHA — you must complete a fresh registration.
Dependant turned away: To add or remove a dependant, use the household profile on sha.go.ke, not *147#.
Someone requesting payment: SHA has stated that registration is free, and their staff will never request money or M-Pesa PINs to provide services. Report any such requests immediately.
Call the SHA toll-free line on 0800 720 601 or dial 147 — both are free from any Kenyan network.
SHA's headquarters is located at the Ground Floor, SHA Building, Ragati Road, Nairobi .

FORTRESS-SSA Master's Scholarship 2026/2027 at Moi University, Kenya – Fully Funded Postgraduate Opportunity for African Students
items.description: The FORTRESS-SSA consortium is inviting applications from eligible African students and public health professionals for its 2026/2027 Master's Scholarship
content: The FORTRESS-SSA consortium is inviting applications from eligible African students and public health professionals for its 2026/2027 Master’s Scholarship Programme at Moi University, Kenya . The scholarship provides an opportunity for qualified candidates to pursue advanced postgraduate studies in public health, infectious diseases, and field epidemiology.
The programme is designed to strengthen Africa’s capacity to prevent, detect, investigate, and respond to infectious disease threats through advanced education, research, and professional training.

One fully funded scholarship is available for a period of up to two years at the Moi University School of Public Health. Successful applicants will receive financial support covering tuition fees, international return airfare, monthly living expenses, medical insurance, and selected research and learning materials.

The scholarship is particularly suitable for African public health professionals, healthcare practitioners, researchers, and graduates interested in strengthening disease surveillance, epidemiological research, and public health systems across the continent.

The FORTRESS-SSA scholarship aims to develop skilled African professionals capable of addressing infectious disease challenges through specialised postgraduate training and evidence-based public health interventions.
Hosted by the Moi University School of Public Health in Eldoret, Kenya, the programme offers specialised academic training in three key areas:

The scholarship supports the development of expertise required to strengthen national and regional health systems, improve infectious disease preparedness, and promote effective public health responses across African countries.
The selected scholar will undertake a relevant Master’s degree programme during the 2026/2027 academic year.
Applicants can apply for scholarship support to pursue one of the following postgraduate programmes at Moi University:

The Master of Public Health programme focuses on developing advanced knowledge and professional competencies in public health practice, population health, disease prevention, health promotion, and public health policy.
The programme is suitable for professionals seeking to contribute to healthcare planning, health systems strengthening, disease prevention, and public health research.
2. Master of Science in Field Epidemiology and Laboratory Training (FELTP)
This programme focuses on strengthening practical expertise in field epidemiology, laboratory surveillance, disease investigation, and outbreak response.
It is relevant to professionals interested in disease surveillance, epidemiological investigations, laboratory systems, and the prevention and control of infectious diseases.
3. Master of Science in Infectious Diseases and Global Health (IDGH)
The programme provides specialised training in infectious diseases, global health challenges, disease prevention, and research approaches for improving health outcomes.
It is suitable for candidates interested in infectious disease research, public health interventions, and strengthening healthcare responses to emerging and existing disease threats.
To qualify for the FORTRESS-SSA Master’s Scholarship, applicants must satisfy the following requirements:
Priority Consideration: Preference will be given to applicants currently employed by National Ministries of Health or Public Health Institutes.
Gender Inclusion: Women are particularly encouraged to apply.
Applicants should ensure that they meet the academic, professional, and institutional requirements before submitting their scholarship applications.
The FORTRESS-SSA scholarship offers comprehensive financial support to the successful candidate for up to two years of Master’s degree studies.
This funding package is intended to reduce financial barriers to postgraduate education and enable the selected scholar to concentrate on academic training and research.
Interested candidates must prepare a complete scholarship application containing the following documents:
Applicants should ensure that all documents are complete, accurate, and properly prepared before submission.
Applications must be submitted electronically through email.
Eligible candidates are required to send their complete application documents in the same email to both designated recipients:
Dean, School of Public Health, Moi University
Applicants must ensure that both email addresses are included in the same application submission.
Candidates are encouraged to use a clear email subject identifying the FORTRESS-SSA Master’s Scholarship application and ensure that all required documents are attached.
For additional information, applicants should consult the official scholarship announcement published by Moi University.
The deadline for submitting applications for the FORTRESS-SSA Master’s Scholarship for the 2026/2027 academic year is 15 December 2026 .
Interested applicants are encouraged to begin preparing their documentation early, particularly the research statement, certified academic certificates, and proof of admission.
Late or incomplete applications may not be considered.

The scholarship offers an important opportunity for African professionals to acquire advanced postgraduate qualifications while contributing to the development of stronger public health systems across the continent.

Through specialised training in public health, field epidemiology, and infectious diseases, the programme supports the development of professionals equipped to address emerging health threats, strengthen disease surveillance, and improve public health decision-making.
The post-study commitment to National Ministries of Health and Public Health Institutes also promotes the application of acquired knowledge within African health institutions.
